grammar[0].fact: Hamburg’s *Hafenrundfahrt* leaves from the Landungsbrücken every few minutes. The harbour has been a free port for centuries, and its founding date, 7 May 1189, comes from a document known to be a fake. Hamburg throws the birthday party anyway.

grammar[1].blocks[1].blocks[0].text: *man* means “you, people” in general: Hier darf *man* nicht parken. Wie sagt *man* das auf Deutsch? It takes the er-form: man *sagt*, man *kann*.
grammar[1].blocks[2].title: alle or alles?
grammar[1].blocks[2].text: *alle* are people — they: Alle *sind* da. *alles* is things — it: Alles *ist* fertig.
grammar[1].blocks[3].title: Words for the practice page
grammar[1].fact: Germans answer email fast and take its formality seriously: *Sehr geehrte* for strangers, *Hallo* for colleagues, and *Mit freundlichen Grüßen* at the foot. And many firms have an out-of-office rule: no work mail after hours. Maya’s boss has not read it.

opener.caption: Die Landungsbrücken in Hamburg, mit dem Hafen dahinter.
reading.intro: Maya has spent the weekend in Hamburg, and on Sunday evening she writes to Lena about it. She works in a small office now, and she does what everyone does with email: she clicks the first name the machine offers her.
reading.photos[0].caption: Die Elbphilharmonie: unten ein Lager, oben Musik.
reading.photos[1].caption: Eine Hafenrundfahrt: Das Wetter ist schön, das bleibt nicht so.
reading.en: **From:** Maya. **To:** Everyone. **Subject:** My weekend! · Dear Lena, the weekend was great! First on Saturday we went to the fish market, because you can have such a good breakfast there. Then we took a harbour tour. · After that we went to a concert. On Monday I’m not going to the office, because I’m ill. That’s not true, of course! But no one notices anything. My boss knows nothing, he’s never there. Everyone here does as they please. See you soon, Maya. · Two minutes later, a reply from Nora: · Nora: Maya? You’ve sent that to everyone. To EVERYONE. Including the boss. · Five minutes later, a reply from Jan in accounting: · Jan: Which concert? Is the Elbphilharmonie good? Just asking. · And then, at nine in the evening, the reply from the boss: · Chef: Dear Maya, get well soon! Since you’ll be ill on Monday, please come in early on Tuesday. You’ll then do something new: from now on, you’ll write all our emails to everyone. You have talent. · Chef: P.S. I was at the concert on Saturday too. Row 5. I saw you.
reading.fact: The Elbphilharmonie opened in 2017 on top of an old harbour warehouse. It was seven years late and cost about ten times the first plan, and Hamburg complained loudly until the first concert, then queued for tickets.

document.caption: Eine Konzertkarte: Wann, wo, wie viel?
document.intro: A real concert ticket, from Offenburg in 2010. It tells you everything in about eight lines: who plays, when, where, and what it cost. *Stehplätze* are standing places, *Rückgabe* and *Umtausch* mean returning and exchanging. The small print says you can’t.
document.fact: Germany has more than 130 publicly funded orchestras, more than any other country, so tickets for a concert are often cheaper than you would expect. Ask for *Restkarten* at the door, last-minute tickets, especially if you are under 30.
